1.script: LIFE IN MONGOLIA How People Live in the World's Most Extreme Land of Nomads Imagine living in a country where there are more horses than people. Where winter temperatures can fall far below freezing. Where a family can live inside a round felt tent called a ger, surrounded by nothing but grassland stretching toward the horizon. Where the nearest neighbor might be many kilometers away. And where surviving the winter is not just difficult. It can determine whether an entire family has a future. This is Mongolia.

67.script: For Mongolians, the historical legacy is complicated but powerful. The empire is part of the country's national story. It is a democratic country trying to build a modern economy while preserving its cultural identity.

68.script: FROM SOCIALISM TO MODERN MONGOLIA For most of the twentieth century, Mongolia was closely aligned with the Soviet Union. The country followed a socialist political and economic system. That period deeply influenced architecture, education, politics and urban life. Then, in the early 1990s, Mongolia underwent a peaceful democratic transition. The country moved toward a market economy and democratic political institutions. The transformation was difficult. But it opened Mongolia to the wider world. Today, Mongolia balances relationships with its two enormous neighbors, Russia and China, while also maintaining strong connections with countries around the world.

These questions are becoming increasingly important as Mongolia tries to develop without losing the environment that has supported nomadic life for centuries.

71.script: A LIFE BETWEEN TWO WORLDS Perhaps the most fascinating thing about Mongolia is that two very different ways of life can exist at the same time. In one part of the country, a herder can wake before sunrise, open the door of a ger and look across thousands of kilometers of empty landscape. A few hours away, a university student can sit inside a modern cafe in Ulaanbaatar using a laptop and smartphone.
